title: Outer billiards around analytic tables with flat points
credit: Moser's boundedness question (J. Moser, Stable and Random Motions, 1973); Douady (thesis, 1982); Sorrentino arXiv:2610.06418 (2026) for the C^1-generic case.
results: I checked the singularity claim. At a flat point of order k the radius of curvature satisfies rho(theta)~|theta|^{-k/(k+1)} (|theta|^{-2/3} for x^4+y^4), and the tangency point q(p) is only C^{1/(k+1)} across the tangent lines at the flat points. So T and the limiting map at infinity are genuinely non-smooth, and KAM does not apply directly. The claim is correct.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06418 (Sorrentino, 2026 preprint): cited for C^1-generic unbounded orbits (centrally symmetric tables only); motivation only, the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser-Douady). Polygons, semicircles and generic C^1 shapes can have orbits that escape to infinity. What if the table is analytic and strictly convex, but its curvature vanishes at a few points, like the superellipse x^4+y^4 ≤ 1? Decide whether every orbit stays bounded.
math: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a strictly convex body whose boundary is a real-analytic closed curve with curvature vanishing at at least one point (hence, by analyticity, at finitely many). For $p\in\mathbb R^2\setminus K$, let $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the tangency point of the tangent line from $p$ that has $K$ on its left. Is every $T$-orbit bounded, for every such $K$? If not, characterize the $K$ with unbounded orbits, e.g. by the vanishing orders of the curvature or by symmetry. First test case: $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$.
